Susannah Spurgeon
sū-zan'ə spĕr'jən
n. (Susannah Spurgeon, née Thompson, 1832–1903, wife of C. H. Spurgeon and founder of the Book Fund for poor ministers)
Hebrew Shoshannah, a lily; English Spurgeon, of uncertain origin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Susannah Thompson was a London merchant's daughter who first heard the young Charles Spurgeon preach at New Park Street Chapel in 1853, was converted under his ministry, and married him in January 1856. Their twin sons, Charles and Thomas, were born that September; both became Baptist ministers. From about 1868 she was an invalid, often confined to her room for long periods, and could seldom hear her husband preach. In 1875, after reading the first volume of his Lectures to My Students, she wished that every poor minister in England could have a copy, and her husband challenged her to see to it. The Book Fund she founded distributed, by her own hand and correspondence, some two hundred thousand volumes to pastors who could not afford books, in every denomination and many countries, and her accounts of it, Ten Years of My Life in the Service of the Book Fund, show a woman who turned her suffering into ministry to ministers. After her husband's death in 1892 she completed his four-volume Autobiography and founded a Baptist chapel at Bexhill. She is the woman of Proverbs, of whom “her husband also, and he praiseth her” (Pro 31:28), and the friend of Paul's need: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a wife as the lawful consort of a man, and an invalid as a person who is weak or infirm.

expand to see more

WIFE, n. The lawful consort of man; a woman who is united to man in the lawful bonds of wedlock.

INVALID, n. A person who is weak and infirm; a person sickly or indisposed.

FUND, n. A stock or capital; a sum of money appropriated as the foundation of some commercial or other operation.

Pro 31:28 — "Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her."

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Modern Corruption

A minister's invalid wife who supplied two hundred thousand books to poor ministers.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Susannah Spurgeon is sometimes recruited as an example of a woman finding her own ministry apart from her husband. Her own account is the opposite: she served her husband's calling and the calling of other pastors, from an invalid's room, and called it the joy of her life. Scripture's praise of the godly wife is her portrait: “a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30).

The principle to recover is that suffering does not end usefulness. The Book Fund grew from a sickroom, and its letters show “in her tongue is the law of kindness” (Pro 31:26). A church that sees in chronic illness only loss has not considered how often God has worked through the bedridden.
